Indexes speed up database queries by providing a data structure—often a B-tree—that allows the database to locate rows much faster than by scanning every record in a table. Instead of checking every entry, the database can navigate the index to jump directly to the relevant data, reducing the number of disk reads or memory accesses required.

However, indexes hurt performance in several ways. They consume extra storage space and slow down write operations, such as inserts, updates, and deletes, because the index must be updated every time the underlying data changes. Additionally, if a query is already fast enough or if the table is small, the overhead of maintaining the index may outweigh the benefit of using it. Excessive indexing can also clutter the database and slow down overall system performance.

In autoregressive generation, a transformer predicts the next token one at a time. Without a cache, each new token would require recomputing the key and value (K and V) tensors for every previous token in the sequence. This is computationally expensive because the model would redo the same work for the entire history every single step.

The KV cache stores the previously computed K and V tensors for all tokens generated so far. When generating the next token, the model only needs to compute the new token's query (Q), key (K), and value (V). It then uses the cached K and V from all prior steps to perform the attention calculation. This reduces the per-step computation from a full re-evaluation of the entire sequence to just a single new token's contribution.

The result is a significant speedup in generation, as the model avoids redundant matrix multiplications and attention operations. The trade

Optimistic locking assumes that conflicts are rare, so it doesn't lock data during a transaction. Instead, it checks for changes when the transaction is committed. If the data has changed since it was read, the transaction fails and is retried. A practical example is a web application where multiple users edit a shared document; the system only checks for conflicts when the user clicks "Save," allowing for high concurrency.

Pessimistic locking assumes conflicts are likely, so it locks the data as soon as it is read or modified. This prevents other transactions from accessing the data until the first transaction is complete. A practical example is an airline booking system where a seat is locked the moment a user selects it, ensuring no other user can book that same seat until the transaction is finalized.

When packet loss occurs, TCP interprets it as a sign of congestion. To recover, it reduces its sending rate—often by halving the congestion window—and enters a recovery phase to gradually increase the rate again.

Latency is managed through mechanisms like Round-Trip Time (RTT) estimation. TCP monitors the time it takes for packets to travel to the receiver and back. If latency increases significantly, it suggests the network is becoming congested. TCP uses this feedback to adjust its sending rate, aiming to keep the network utilization high while minimizing delays and avoiding the point where packets are dropped.

Together, these responses ensure that TCP adapts to changing network conditions, balancing throughput with stability and responsiveness.

Optimistic and pessimistic locking are two strategies for managing concurrent access to database data.

Pessimistic locking assumes conflicts are likely, so it locks data before it is read or modified. This prevents other transactions from touching the data until the first transaction completes. Optimistic locking assumes conflicts are rare, so it does not lock data upfront. Instead, it checks for conflicts at commit time, often using version numbers or timestamps. To recover, it reduces its sending rate—often by halving the congestion window—and enters a recovery phase to gradually increase the rate again.

Latency is managed through mechanisms like Round-Trip Time (RTT) estimation. TCP monitors the time it takes for packets to travel to the receiver and back. If latency increases significantly, it suggests the network is becoming congested. TCP uses this feedback to adjust its sending rate, aiming to keep the network utilization high while minimizing delays and avoiding the point where packets are dropped.

Together, these responses ensure that TCP adapts to changing network conditions, balancing throughput with stability and responsiveness.

Indexes speed up database queries by providing a data structure—often a B-tree—that allows the database to locate rows much faster than by scanning every record in a table. Instead of checking every entry, the database can navigate the index to jump directly to the relevant data, reducing the number of disk reads or memory accesses required.

However, indexes hurt performance in several ways. They consume extra storage space and slow down write operations, such as inserts, updates, and deletes, because the index must be updated every time the underlying data changes. Additionally, if a query is already fast enough or if the table is small, the overhead of maintaining the index may outweigh the benefit of using it. Excessive indexing can also clutter the database and slow down overall system performance.

The KV cache solves this by storing the K and V tensors from all previously processed tokens. This reduces the per-step computation from a full re-evaluation of the sequence to a much smaller incremental update, making generation significantly faster and more efficient.

TCP congestion control responds to packet loss and latency by adjusting its sending rate to match the available network capacity. When packet loss occurs, TCP interprets it as a sign of congestion and reduces its sending rate, often by cutting the congestion window in half. This is typically handled through mechanisms like slow start, congestion avoidance, and fast retransmit/fast recovery.

Latency is managed through round-trip time (RTT) measurements. TCP uses these measurements to estimate how long it takes for data to travel to the receiver and back. If latency increases, it suggests the network is becoming congested or overloaded. TCP uses this feedback to adjust its sending rate, ensuring it does not overwhelm the network while still maintaining a high throughput.

In summary, TCP uses packet loss as a primary signal to back off and reduce its rate, while latency provides a secondary signal to gauge network health and adjust its sending behavior accordingly.
